title: How Water Slides Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the history and physics of water slides. They trace early precursors (aqueduct workers in Rome and Egypt, natural slides, a 1903 Minnesota water toboggan), then the 1970s origins of the modern water park, centered on George Malay, Wet 'n Wild in Orlando and its wave pool and lazy river, and the fiberglass Kamikaze slide. They explain the physics of potential and kinetic energy, friction and water, inertia on curves, the water break invented by Jeff Henry, the tallest slides at Schlitterbahn in Kansas City, water blasters and water coasters, and the pump, filtration, and closed-circuit water systems. They cover Action Park in New Jersey and water park injury statistics, then listener mail from Tyler Murphy about teaching physics with a Slinky.

segments.title: Opening banter about water slides
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open by talking about enjoying water parks and mention Schlitterbahn in Kansas City.

segments.title: Early water slides and first water toboggan
segments.summary: They discuss possible early water slides, including aqueduct workers in Rome and Egypt and natural slides, then Herbert Selna's 1903 water toboggan in Minnesota and a 1930s English flat-bottomed boat slide.

segments.title: George Malay and the origins of the water park
segments.summary: Concrete water slides of the 1970s are described, followed by George Malay's idea to combine slides, wave pools and kids' attractions. Investors doubt the idea before he raises about three million dollars.

segments.title: Wet 'n Wild in Orlando
segments.summary: Wet 'n Wild opens in Orlando with a wave pool as its centerpiece. It loses money at first because visitors are used to roller coaster parks. The lazy river, borrowed from another park, becomes a success, and the enclosed river is shaped like infinity.

segments.title: Copycat names, Kamikaze slide and fiberglass
segments.summary: Water parks of the 1970s copied one another's ride names. The Kamikaze was the first very tall US water slide, made of fiberglass, which allowed slides to rise above ground. It was placed as a visible landmark. Parks also made money on concessions and swimsuits.

segments.title: Physics of water slides
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain potential and kinetic energy, gravity, friction reduced by water, and how steeper drops reduce friction. They describe inertia on curves and why high side walls and fully enclosed tubes were added.

segments.title: Water break, tallest slides and water coasters
segments.summary: The water break was invented by Jeff Henry, who started with a regular slide at a family campground. Schlitterbahn's Verrückt is the tallest, at 168 feet 7 inches, followed by Kilimanjaro and Insano in Brazil. The water coaster and water blasters use water jets to move riders uphill.

segments.title: Water slide construction and water park filtration
segments.summary: Water slides are assembled from fiberglass pieces designed by specialist companies. Water is pumped to the top through a closed circuit, filtered through sand and gravel, and backwashed. Check valves keep water in the pipes overnight.

segments.title: Action Park and water park safety
segments.summary: Action Park in New Jersey is described as dangerous but popular, and it was reopened by its former owners after a viral documentary. A New Jersey study found water park attractions caused far more amusement park accidents than roller coasters.

segments.title: Lazy river hide and seek and Tyler Murphy's Slinky mail
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh share memories of playing hide and seek in the lazy river. Listener Tyler Murphy, a teacher, writes in about using a Slinky to demonstrate how information travels through a wave.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to social media, email, and the website for more on water slides.
